findings.claim: Flashcard answer "Level 1 (L1) cache." (question: "Which level of cache is the smallest and fastest?")
findings.truth: The computing fact is right: L1 cache is the smallest and fastest level. The only concern is the literal string "Level 1", which sits on the checker's banned-string list. That ban stops board band names leaking into lessons; here it is ordinary cache terminology and must NOT be reworded, because "Level 1 cache" is the standard name. Recorded so an automated banned-string sweep is not read as a real failure, and so a later pass does not rewrite a correct card.
findings.evidence: CHECK_PROMPT_GENERIC.md banned-string list; raw/L02.txt flashcard 5; spec 1.1.2 lists cache size as a CPU performance characteristic without naming levels

findings.claim: "ASCII, which uses 7 bits per character and can therefore represent 128 different characters"
findings.truth: Correct as written. ASCII is a 7-bit code with 128 characters. The spec separately states that binary representation of ASCII in the exam will use 8 bits, and the lesson is already consistent with that: its worked text calculation uses 8-bit codes (200 x 8 = 1,600 bits = 200 bytes) and it teaches that one byte stores one character. No edit needed; recorded so a later pass does not 'correct' the 7-bit statement, which is right.
findings.evidence: spec 1.2.4 Data storage - Characters: 'Binary representation of ASCII in the exam will use 8 bits'; raw/L06.txt n23 and key fact n24

findings.claim: Two cards test the same idea: "What is meant by saying RAM is volatile?" -> "It loses its contents when the power is turned off." and "What does 'volatile' mean?" -> "The memory loses all its contents when the power is switched off."
findings.truth: Both cards are factually correct and their answer strings differ, so the deck passes the unique-answer rule. The overlap is redundancy, not an error. Replacing one would mean authoring new content rather than fixing a fact, so no edit is proposed.
findings.evidence: raw/L04.txt flashcards 4 and 6; validator rule is exact-duplicate answer text within a deck

findings.claim: Knowledge check 5 asks students to match "Run-length encoding" to "Stores a repeated value with a count of its repeats"; run-length encoding and Huffman coding also appear as distractors in check 3.
findings.truth: Not a scope error. The spec's Not-required line bars the ability to CARRY OUT specific compression algorithms; it does not bar knowing the principle of lossless techniques, and the lesson keeps both methods inside an optional collapsible. The checks only test the principle, so they are harmless. Recorded so this is not re-raised as an over-teaching finding.
findings.evidence: spec 1.2.5 Compression - Not required: 'Ability to carry out specific compression algorithms'; raw/L08.txt collapsible n9-n10 and knowledge checks 3 and 5

summary: No fixes required. Every calculation in the unit was recomputed and is correct: 156 = 10011100; 10011100 = 156; 217 = 11011001 = D9; 00101010 = 42; 53 + 22 = 01001011 (75); 255 + 1 overflows the byte to 00000000; 00010100 shifted left 2 = 01010000 (20 x 4 = 80); 2F = 47; 10011100 = 9C; 8 x 200 x 300 = 480,000 bits = 60,000 bytes; 4 x 50 x 40 = 8,000 bits; 44,100 x 30 x 16 = 21,168,000 bits = 2,646,000 bytes (about 2.6 MB); 3 bits = 8 colours; 24-bit = over 16 million. All 20 answer keys are right: every mcq and fill correct index points at the true option, and all 12 match questions are valid permutations with correct pairings. Facts verified against the spec: the four Von Neumann registers and their address-versus-data roles, the three CPU performance characteristics, embedded-system characteristics, RAM/ROM volatility and the bootstrap, the six storage characteristics, the decimal unit ladder (1 KB = 1,000 bytes) with the spec's own 1,024 allowance quoted, the six named forms of attack, the seven named prevention methods, the five operating-system functions and the three utility programs. External checks confirmed CD 700 MB / single-layer DVD 4.7 GB / single-layer Blu-ray 25 GB, IPv4 32 bits and IPv6 128 bits, a 12-hex-digit MAC address, and the three original Computer Misuse Act 1990 offences; the Data Protection Act 2018 and Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988 are named and dated correctly. The unit makes no exam claim at all - no paper, timing, mark total, tier or board name appears anywhere in student-facing text - and all 72 practice tariffs (1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 8 marks) are consistent with their own mark schemes and with a single 8-mark extended response. The four TCP/IP layer names are correctly omitted, matching the spec's not-required list.
